matters.title: 3. Consideration of Request to Rezone Ainsworth's Addition, Block 3 from the R-1 (One-family Residential) zoning district to the B-3 (General Business) zoning district. A) Public Comment B) Action on the Item
matters.text:
Agenda Item Details 

 Meeting 
 Mar 04, 2024 - Regular City Commission Meeting 
 Category 
 E. SPECIAL ORDERS OF BUSINESS 
 Subject 
 3. Consideration of Request to Rezone Ainsworth's Addition, Block 3 from the R-1 (One-family Residential) zoning district to the B-3 (General Business) zoning district. A) Public Comment B) Action on the Item 
 Type 
 Action 
 Preferred Date 
 Mar 04, 2024 
 Absolute Date 
 Mar 04, 2024 
 Fiscal Impact 
 No 
 Recommended Action 
 Motion to deny the requested rezoning of Ainsworth' Addition, Block 3, from R-1 (One-family Residential) to B-3 (General Business). 

 BACKGROUND : 

 An application (ATTACHMENT I) has been submitted by Bruce Burton on behalf of Burton Land Holdings, LLC, to rezone Ainsworth’s Addition, Block 3 from R-1 (One-family Residential) to B-3 (General Business). 

 The subject property consists of 31 platted lots and occupies approximately 3.8 acres of land, inclusive of roughly 0.28 acres of internal alleyways which have not been vacated. A single-family dwelling and associated accessory buildings occupy the property’s northwest corner while the remainder is undeveloped. An aerial photograph of the site is included as ATTACHMENT II . 

 The subject property has been substantially under the same ownership since 1977 and, aside from the residential dwelling, has been used as supplemental material storage and a snow dump for Burton Excavating. The material storage and snow dump initially occupied a small portion of the property; however, its footprint and intensity has gradually expanded over time. 

 In mid-2021, a noise complaint resulting from the operation of a large-scale inclined soil screen on the property on a Sunday afternoon came into the City’s Community Development Department. Upon follow-up and review, formal notice was provided to the owners that the uses of the property associated with the operations of Burton Excavating were in violation of the property’s R-1 zoning designation and needed to be discontinued. The property owner exercised their right to request a use variance from the Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) to continue the activities on the property. The ZBA held a meeting on October 21, 2021, where the application was considered. After hearing from staff, the applicant, and members of the public, the Board voted to deny the application on a 6-1 vote. An excerpt of the minutes from that meeting is included as ATTACHMENT III and the staff report generated in connection with that request is ATTACHMENT IV . 

 In the time since the ZBA meeting, the property owner has evaluated different approaches to expanding the use of the property beyond that of a single-family homesite and have brought forward this proposal to rezone the property from R-1 to B-3. 

 A copy of the permitted use list in the R-1 district is included as ATTACHMENT V and a copy of the permitted use list in the B-3 district is included as ATTACHMENT VI . 

 An excerpt of the existing zoning map showing the location of the subject property and its surroundings is included as ATTACHMENT VII . 

 ANALYSIS : 

 As noted previously, the applicant is seeking the rezoning to B-3 to establish a storage facility on the property. Although the rezoning is being sought for a specific use case, it is important to bear in mind that a rezoning to B-3 would permit all uses permitted in the district to occupy the property, not just the one(s) the applicant intends to occupy it. Further, as zoning is essentially permanent and runs with the land, a future owner of the property would be entitled to modify the use of the property as they saw fit, provided of course that the new use was permitted in the B-3 district. 

 As a result of these factors, the staff analysis will be more general in nature rather than focus on the applicant’s stated use case for the property. 

 When determining the appropriateness of a rezoning request, the first step in gathering information would be to review the City’s Future Land Use Map (FLU Map). The FLU Map is a component of the City’s Master Plan and sets forth a vision for the uses of land within the City with a forward-looking point of view. The Master Plan is assembled with a great deal of public input so significant deviations from it should be given very careful thought and analysis prior to being approved. In this case, the FLU designates the subject property as having a Low-Density Residential designation along with a majority of the property in the immediate vicinity. An annotated excerpt of the FLU Map is included as ATTACHMENT VIII . 

 With the FLU Map calling for the subject property to remain in residential use into the future, the applicant’s rezoning request represents a significant departure from the vision. If rezoned, the subject property would become an isolated area of commercial zoning 6/10 mile away from the nearest other property with a commercial zoning designation. Of note, this measure excludes the Sault Tribe casino complex, which is zoned RSV, a single-family residential zoning designation. By virtue of its trust land status, the Tribe is exempt from compliance with local zoning requirements. Were the land occupied by the casino complex commercially zoned, the 6/10 mile figure would be reduced to ½ mile, still a significant distance. 

 When changes to zoning take place in isolation from other similarly zoned areas, it is open to being labeled as spot zoning. According to MSU Extension, spot zoning is generally considered to include the following criteria, all of which need to be satisfied: 

 The area is small compared to districts surrounding the parcel in question. 

 The new district allows land uses inconsistent with those allowed in the vicinity. 

 The new district would confer a special benefit on the individual property owner not commonly enjoyed by the owners of similar property. 

 The request conflicts with the policies in the text of the master plan and the future land use map. 

 Source: https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/how_to_spot_a_spot_zoning 

 In the opinion of staff the applicant’s request meets each of the four criteria to be considered a spot zoning. 

 Another area of review would be the compatibility of the uses permitted within the proposed district with those in the surrounding area. The B-3 zoning district is primarily focused on retail-type uses and is the dominant zoning designation along the entire length of Ashmun Street south of the power canal as well as the entire length of the I-75 Business Spur. These areas are associated with higher traffic volumes, late day commercial activities, and additional noise over and above what one would expect in a predominantly residential area. In the professional opinion of staff, the types of uses and their associated characteristics would not be in harmony with the uses established and anticipated in the area surrounding the subject property. While commercial uses are the primary type of uses permitted in the B-3, it also allows mobile home parks and apartments of four or more units. 

 Presently, the dwelling on the subject property is served by a private water line extending south from the water main on Marquette Avenue. Wastewater disposal is via septic system. There is a 16” water main which runs down the east edge of the subject proper, however, sewer is not immediately available as the closest location to tie into is in Marquette Avenue. The sewer is near enough capacity that it may not be able to support the maximum development potential of approximately 13 single-family dwellings, however, is more likely to be able to support a lesser number. With a fewer number of dwellings on larger parcels, septic systems may be able to serve any future dwellings constructed on the site. Most certainly, additional infrastructure such as roads would need to be constructed and not all of the property may be developed due to the presence of wetlands near the rear, however, there are opportunities to expand the use of the property within the confines of its existing zoning designation and in ways which are likely to be more compatible with the surrounding uses already established. It is not known the availability status of the other utilities, however it is presumed that at least electricity is available. 

 Overall, it is the position of staff that the proposed rezoning is incompatible with the surrounding uses. 

 PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION : 

 At their regular meeting held on February 22, 2024, the Planning Commission recommended that this request be denied in a unanimous vote. 

 COMMUNITY OUTREACH : 

 All required notices have been mailed and published as required by State Statute. As of 2/20/24, four contacts have been received by the Community Development Department as it relates to this request. Two comments were received in opposition to the request and one comment was received in support of the request. In the interest of full disclosure, the comment in favor of the was submitted by a member of the Burton family. A fourth contact was to seek additional information about the request. A letter of objection was received and is included as ATTACHMENT IX . 

 FISCAL IMPACT : 

 There is no fiscal impact associated with this rezoning request. 

 ALTERNATIVES : 

 List alternatives to the recommended action. 

 The City Commission has the following options to consider on this matter: 

 Adopt ordinance with modifications. 

 Direct staff to return with more information. 

 Approve the First Reading of the Ordinance and schedule Second Reading for the March 18, 2024, City Commission meeting. 

 Direct staff to schedule a Public Hearing for the April 1, 2024, City Commission meeting. (15-day statutory notice required) 

 Other Alternative 

 Take no action. 

 Motion & Voting 

 Motion to deny the requested rezoning of Ainsworth' Addition, Block 3, from R-1 (One-family Residential) to B-3 (General Business).

Motion by Jodi Bosbous-Rath, second by Jay Gage.

 Final Resolution: Motion Carried

 Yea: Don Gerrie, Jodi Bosbous-Rath, Jay Gage, Andrew Rubinstein

 Nay: Ray Bauer, Steve Habusta, Scott Marble

2. Motion to authorize the purchase from Stryker of seven Lifepack 1000 AEDs at a cost of $21,921.55.
3. Motion to amend the Police capital equipment budget with an increase of $5,000 in funding to come from the General Fund. 

 BACKGROUND : 

 The police department desires to have each of its seven patrol vehicles equipped with an up-to-date Automated External Defibrillator (AED); the Lifepack 1000. 

 The AED units that the police department currently have aren't compatible with equipment used by Sault Fire and MyMichigan Hospital, the Lifepack 1000 is. 

 Purchasing new AED's for the police department was included in the 2023-2024 CIP plan. 

 Stryker is the sole-source provider in the hospital, emergency response services, and emergency response training markets in the U.S. and Canada for the Lifepack 1000 AED. 

 ANALYSIS : 

 The police department doesn't have enough AEDs to equip each patrol vehicle with a unit, thus, vehicles can and are being deployed without an AED on board. Additionally, the police department needs adult and infant/child AED pads for each unit. 

 The AED units the police department currently have are old units and either near, at, or past end of life. 

 The AED units and equipment the police department currently have aren't compatible with equipment utilized by Sault Fire and MyMichigan Hospital and as a result, when either of those two agencies take over care of a patient from the police department, they must deploy their own AED equipment. This doesn't promote continuity/transfer of care.

 FISCAL IMPACT : 

 Seven Lifepack 1000 units, with adult and infant/child pads, will cost $21,921.55.

Prices have increased since the CIP budget was established and additional costs are related to needed AED pads. A budget amendment at add $5,000 to 101-902-977.301 is requested to fund this AED purchase. 

 For reference only, the recent police department men's bathroom floor capital project, also funded by the General Fund, came in at $3,796.00 under budget.

Motion to approve the capital expenditure budget for the Airport Layout Plan for $55,500 with funding to come from TIFA3.
Motion to award the contract to Prein & Newholf in the amount of $55,500.00. 

 BACKGROUND : 

 At the May 6, 2024 City Commission meeting, commissioners requested to table it and send it back to the TIFA III board for further discussion. The TIFA III Board scheduled a special meeting on Friday, May 10th in which they unanimously voted to approve the Airport Layout Plan after receiving further information on the state requirements of it. 

 On May 20, 2019 the City Commission awarded a bid for professional engineering services at Sanderson Field from Prein & Newhof to start July 1, 2019 for a term of 5 years. 

 On August 15, 2022, the City Commission approved Great Circle Aviation’s presentation and proposal for the NPIAS Application. 

 According to a timeline presented to the Airport Advisory Board [AAB], the NPIAS application must be completed with an Airport Layout Plan by July 1, 2024, which is also the term limit of the contract with Prien & Newhof. NPIAS applications are only reviewed every two years. By approving the updated Airport Layout Plan, the NPIAS application will be completed and ready to submit. If approved for NPIAS, this would allow Sanderson Field to still qualify for the final years of the Biden Infrastructure Law to update the taxi-way. 

 For Sanderson Field to apply for any funding, including state funding, and stay compliant within the state an Airport Layout Plan must be completed every 5-years. The last plan was updated 7 years ago. 

 Prien & Newhof had originally proposed an $85,700 cost to update the plan, but after the FBO, Airport Manager and EDC staff met with them, a price of $55,500 was updated. Due to the contract with Prien & Newhof, an RFP is not required and there is only one other company in the state that would be able to do the same work. 

 At the April 11, 2024 AAB meeting, the board requested TIFA III to fund the updated plan to proceed with the NPIAS application timeline and state requirements. The AAB also communicated previously this year they would have liked to apply for a grant to cover this cost, however, that money would not be available in time for the NPIAS application to be submitted. 

 At the April 25, 2024, TIFA III meeting, the board voted unanimously to approve the update of the ALP.

 Recommended Action 
 Motion to waive the competitive bidding process. 
Motion to approve the purchase of one Stryker MTS Power Load system from Stryker Corporation, a Michigan company, in the amount of $33,912.31 

 BACKGROUND : 

 The request to purchase a Stryker Power Load system was made in the capital improvement projects for FY 2024/25. The request was approved to purchase one power load system, which would be installed in A-155 which is currently equipped with a manual cot securing device. The power load system is a device that physically lifts and secures a patient cot into the back of an ambulance, reducing the potential for patient drops or injuries to our staff. This devices is part of a system that works directly with our current powered patient cots. The purchase price does include a 3 year preventative maintenance plan. The Stryker MTS Power Load system is a proprietary device and is a sole source item. The quote provided includes installation in our ambulance. 

 Stryker cots are a sole source item, like most medical equipment. There are no external vendors, dealer networks or third parties from which to purchase new Stryker Power Pro cots, all purchases must be made from the manufacturer to ensure warranty coverage of these products. Any after market purchases of cots, or remanufactured ones, would not have warranty coverage or FDA medical approval for use. The Stryker brand power load system is designed to work with our power cots and any change to another manufacturer will require additional components and battery systems, increased stock of wearable components, and the potential for incompatibility between our anchor systems. The city bid process was followed and only one quote was received, from Stryker. 

 ANALYSIS : 

 The pricing quote was prepared by Stryker Corporation and this did not go through a bid process as the results would not change. Stryker Power Load systems are sold from the factory and do not have any third party dealers or vendors. They manufacture the system, lift and cot, to work within ambulances reducing the potential of patient falls or injuries to our staff. Our staff has done significant research and analysis into the patient movement devices we use. In this research, Stryker has the most support within are area of any other manufacturer. Our current fleet cots has been Stryker for a significant period of time, supporting the purchase. 

 COMMUNITY OUTREACH : (if applicable) 

 n/a 

 FISCAL IMPACT : 

 The current quote of $33,912.31 falls under the CIP budget request of $34,000.00, there is no additional anticipated cost with this purchase as quoted. The purchase was budgeted in the CAPITAL EQUIPMENT - AMBULANCE line item 101-902-977.651 and no budget amendment is requested. 

 ALTERNATIVES :

 Direct staff to return with more information.

 Recommended Action 
 Motion to schedule a public hearing for November 18, 2024 during the regularly scheduled City Commission meeting. 

 BACKGROUND : 
 The City has received a request for a tax abatement under the Obsolete Property Rehabilitation Act (OPRA) for 229 Ashmun. The Obsolete Property Rehabilitation Act (OPRA), Public Act 146 of 2000, provides for a tax abatement to encourage the redevelopment of obsolete buildings. The tax abatement is designed to assist in the redevelopment of older buildings in which a facility is contaminated, blighted, or functionally obsolete. The goal is to rehabilitate older buildings into vibrant commercial and mixed-use projects. OPRA tax abatements may be given for those eligible projects that take place on an obsolete property and result in a commercial or mixed-use building project located in only the qualified local units of government, which the City of Sault Ste Marie is. An OPRA tax abatement essentially freezes the existing taxable value on a designated facility for up to 12 years. 
 According to the State Law, a public hearing must be held before Commission consideration. This request is to schedule a public hearing for November 18th. 
 ANALYSIS : 
 Per the requirements listed in the Obsolete Property Rehabilitation Act, the property meets all requirements for an OPRA abatement. The developer has provided more project specifics in their application, which is included. 

 Within the Obsolete Property Rehabilitation Act (OPRA) rehabilitation is defined as:…changes to obsolete commercial property as may be required to restore the property to an economically efficient condition. Rehabilitation includes major renovation and modification including but not necessarily limited to, improvement to floors, correction of deficient or excessive height, new or improved building equipment such as heating ventilation and lighting, improved roof structures and cover, improved wall placement, improved exterior and interior appearance of buildings and other physical changes. For a rehab facility, the OPRA freezes the taxable value of the building at its value before the rehab, and the frozen value and the rehab values are taxed at an adjusted tax rate. Land and personal property cannot be abated under this act and the exemption certificate cannot exceed 12 years. If a certificate is approved by the local unit, the State Tax Commission has 60 days to approve or disapprove the application. 
 Per the requirements listed in the Obsolete Property Rehabilitation Act, the property meets all requirements for an OPRA abatement. The developer has provided more project specifics in their application, which is included. 

 Mr. Brent Blair & Mrs. Lynde Blair requested the full 12 years of the OPRA tax abatement and based on the tax abatement policy under review from the city commission and also based on capital investment, jobs created, wages paid, and housing units created, this project would be eligible for the full 12-year abatement. 

 Currently, the Blairs do not own 229 Ashmun Street, however, based on a reviewed executed purchasing agreement, they will close and occupancy will be immediately after effective November 8th, 2024. The reason for the request for the scheduled public hearing before ownership is due to state deadlines for receiving and approving applications as well as the deadline for assessment values of buildings. 

 COMMUNITY OUTREACH : (if applicable) 
 If approved, a public hearing will be held on November 18th during the regularly scheduled Commission meeting. In addition to the public hearing, all affected taxing jurisdictions will receive a notice of the hearing to provide input. 
 FISCAL IMPACT : 
 The proposed tax incentive would essentially freeze the taxable value at $34,318. With the level of investment and proposed work planned, increasing the taxable value, and a 2% increase assumed, and if the exemption was granted, the total the developer would see is an estimated savings of $113,748.11 over a 12-year timeframe. The other side is that all taxing jurisdictions would forego the tax revenue for the same amount abated.

 Recommended Action 
 Motion to adopt the included Tax Abatement Policy. 

 BACKGROUND and ANALYSIS : 

 Over the past several months, City Administration has been working on the creation of a draft tax abatement policy. The City has had the good fortune of a number of property owners stepping up to improve their properties over the past 10+ years and now seems like a good time to set the stage for these types of activities to continue into the future. 

 Frequently, these property owners are interested in taking advantage of one or more of the state’s tax abatement programs most of which offer some type of tax freeze or reimbursement of eligible costs depending on the program utilized. Since the state’s programs are for the most part flexible in the duration (and thusly the amount) of the abatement, having a policy on their use will ensure that these abatements are administered as fairly and predictably as is possible. 

 Attached to this memo, is the aforementioned draft tax abatement policy. The document sets forth minimum requirements for consideration, criteria by which applications for abatements are to be evaluated, specifics about the application process, and an abatement schedule laying out how abatement timeframes are to be applied. More specifically, the abatement schedule speaks to how the investment amount, job creation, wages, and new housing units impact the duration of the abatement. As an example, the Obsolete Property Rehab Act (OPRA) permits a maximum property tax freeze of 12 years. Based on the proposed abatement schedule, a developer proposing a $2 million investment creating five full-time jobs paying twice minimum wage with no housing units being created would be eligible for 80% of the 12 year timeframe or about 9.6 years. The policy rounds up to the nearest year, so the total offer would be a 10 year abatement. If the same applicant were to add six dwelling units to the package, they’d be able to reach the full 12 years. 

 Just as before, the City Commission retains its role in determining if an abatement request receives favorable consideration or not. It is hoped, however, that the policy will provide greater structure to those discussions as well as guidance to the City Commission. Staff believes that having this type of information publicly available will make the City a more attractive place to invest as it allows potential developers to anticipate the City’s level of participation prior to even engaging us in conversation. Additionally, the policy articulates the City’s goals for new investment. 

 FISCAL IMPACT : 

 There is no fiscal impact directly associated with this policy.

 The City Commission has the following options to consider on this matter: 
 Adopt the policy with modifications. 
 Direct staff to return with more information.

 BACKGROUND : 
 The City has received a request for a tax incentive pursuant to the Obsolete Property Rehabilitation Act (OPRA) for 538 Ashmun Street. The OPRA, Public Act 146 of 2000, provides for a tax incentive to encourage the redevelopment of obsolete buildings. The tax incentive is designed to assist in the redevelopment of older buildings in which a facility is contaminated, blighted or functionally obsolete. The goal is to rehabilitate older buildings into vibrant commercial and mixed-use projects. OPRA tax abatements may be given for those eligible projects that take place on an obsolete property and result in a commercial or mixed-use building project located in only the qualified local units of government, which the City of Sault Ste Marie is. 

 A property for which an OPRA is approved continues to pay property taxes on its pre-project value throughout the duration of the incentive, however, the valuation of the new construction/rehabilitation isn't computed into determining the amount owned until after the OPRA expires. At that point, the full value of the property is taxed, not just the pre-project value. 

 ANALYSIS : 
 Within the OPRA, rehabilitation is defined as:…changes to obsolete commercial property as may be required to restore the property to an economically efficient condition. Rehabilitation includes major renovation and modification, including but not necessarily limited to, improvement to floors, correction of deficient or excessive height, new or improved building equipment such as heating ventilation, and lighting, improved roof structures and cover, improved wall placement, improved exterior and interior appearance of buildings and other physical changes. For a rehabilitated facility, the OPRA freezes the taxable value of the building at its value prior to the rehab, and the frozen value and the rehab values are taxed at an adjusted tax rate. Land and personal property cannot be abated under this act, and the exemption certificate cannot exceed 12 years. If a certificate is approved by the local unit, the State Tax Commission has 60 days to approve or disapprove the application. 
 Per the requirements listed in the Obsolete Property Rehabilitation Act, the property meets all requirements for an OPRA incentive. The developer has provided more project specifics in their application, which is included. This OPRA application has been reviewed by all terms of the tax abatement policy approved on November 4, 2024, and is compliant. The tax abatement policy is attached for review. 
 In the lending industry, a standard debt service ratio of 1.2 is used to determine the viability of a project. The debt service ratio is the measure of a project's ability to generate sufficient cash to cover its debt. Without the OPRA, cash flow projections (attached) suggest an inability to meet the minimum requirements in the first two years of the project making an OPRA incentive a necessary part of the financing package. Of note, without an OPRA incentive, 4Front and the MEDC would be unable to provide funding for the project. 

 COMMUNITY OUTREACH : (if applicable) 
 A public hearing will be conducted during the July 7th Commission meeting. All notices to tax jurisdictions were sent out on June 17, 2025. 

 FISCAL IMPACT : 
 The proposed tax incentive would freeze the taxable value at $59,488 for the next 12 years. Over that period of time, the developer could see a tax savings of $217,973.55 from all tax jurisdictions. The City's share of that would equal approximately $83,500 between the operating and Police/Fire Pension millages. In tax year 2025, this property's contribution to the City's operating millage is $984 with an additional $385 to the Police/Fire Pension. 

 If the OPRA is approved and the project moves forward it is expected the value of the property will increase to an estimated $317,100 in year 1. Computing a 2% annual valuation increase (based on historical state inflation rate multiplier averages) would result in a property valuation of roughly $402,159 at the start of year 13 once the OPRA expires. Once back on at is full value, the property's contribution to the operating millage would be on the order of $6,650 with $2,606 going to the Police/Fire Pension, a 6.7 times increase over today's payments. That increase is applicable to all taxing entities, not just the City. 

 Based on that same 2% value increase, the OPRA would become revenue neutral approximately 10 years after its expiration. 

 If the abatement is not approved and the improvements are not done to the building, the estimated operating millage contribution in 13 years would be $ 1,248 and $489 to the Police/Fire Pension. These figures are based on a $75,445 valuation which results from 13 years of 2% increases in value.

 Type 
 Action, Discussion 

 Commissioner Rubinstein has requested to discuss funding options for the downtown sidewalk snow removal contract. 

 STAFF ANALYSIS AND BACKGROUND: 
 The current ordinance authorizes the Public Works Director to order a property owner or occupant to remove snow and ice from adjacent sidewalks. There has been previous discussion regarding potential updates to the citywide sidewalk clearing ordinance to clarify enforcement procedures and expectations for property owners. 

 Relevant Code Sections: 

 Sec. 22-36. – Adjacent property owners or occupants to obey orders of Director of Public Works to remove obstructions. No person, having the care, either as owner or occupant, of any premises bordered by a paved or graded sidewalk, shall fail to remove promptly therefrom all rubbish, litter, obstructions of any kind, or nuisances of every sort, and snow and ice when ordered by the Director of Public Works. 
 Sec. 22-48. – Designation of sidewalks for snow removal; notice to property owners. The Director of Public Works is hereby authorized to designate from time to time those graded or paved sidewalks from which the snow and ice shall promptly be removed by the owner or occupant of the adjacent premises who has the care of the same. Suitable notice shall be given the public by signs and public announcements of the periods so designated. 

 FISCAL IMPACT: 
 Historically, revenue collected from owner contributions has not been sufficient to fully cover the costs of sidewalk snow removal, with the City covering the remaining balance under the annual contract. The attached worksheet provides a summary of the snowplowing program since its inception in 2014, detailing contributions from business owners and the portion funded by the City. Over that period, the total cost of this program has been approximately $290,400. Business owners have contributed about $169,300, leaving a shortfall of $121,039—an average net cost to the City of roughly $10,000 per year. 

 This program is one of several Downtown Development Authority (DDA) initiatives supported by appropriations from the City’s General Fund and, ultimately, by local taxpayers. Since 2012, the General Fund has contributed approximately $797,500 to the DDA, averaging $72,500 annually. 

 While there have been recent comments suggesting limited City support for the downtown area, financial records demonstrate a long-standing and significant commitment. In addition to direct financial contributions, the City has consistently provided administrative, clerical, and logistical support to ensure the continued success of downtown programs and events. City staff, volunteers, and the Convention & Visitors Bureau have worked together to sustain operations during DDA vacancies, facilitate grant funding, and coordinate business billing for services rendered. 

 For the current fiscal year, the City budgeted a General Fund appropriation of $136,900 for the DDA, which included an additional $35,000 designated for pass-through funding to Headwaters North for administrative support (a function that has since been discontinued). As with all budget decisions, the General Fund must balance many competing priorities; however, the City’s commitment to supporting and strengthening the downtown remains consistent and substantial.

 BACKGROUND AND ANALYSIS: 
 The police department is currently undertaking a project to replace its in-car, body-worn, and interview room camera systems. The existing equipment, purchased in 2016, has exceeded its expected life cycle, resulting in frequent malfunctions and discontinued manufacturer support. Both the in-car and body-worn cameras are experiencing failures, which make it increasingly difficult to maintain reliable operation and secure evidence management. To address these challenges, the City released a Request for Proposals (RFP) on September 18, 2025, with a proposal submission deadline of December 5, 2025, to try and identify and select a vendor that can provide an integrated, modern camera system meeting the department’s operational and technical needs. 

 The current goal for the body-worn camera portion of the larger project is to obtain 15 new cameras and the supporting system , which will replace aging equipment, expand coverage to detective personnel, and provide reliable, secure video capture and storage. A modern system will also enable automated redaction and efficient evidence sharing with the Prosecutor’s Office and partner agencies, improving transparency, accountability, and operational efficiency. 

 The department desires to apply for federal funds through the BJA FY25 Body-Worn Camera Policy and Implementation Program (BWCPIP) to assist specifically with the body-worn camera portion of the replacement project . This funding will reduce the financial impact on the City while allowing the department to implement a reliable, modern system. The grant supports publicly funded law enforcement agencies in establishing or expanding BWC programs, which can strengthen the evidentiary foundation for criminal prosecutions, provide reliable documentation of officer-citizen encounters, and deter assaults on officers. 

 The BWCPIP program includes Category 1: Site-Based Awards , which supports state, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies seeking to establish, expand, and update BWC programs. Applicants under this category must demonstrate a clear plan for phased deployment, policy development, training, and integration of BWCs into agency operations. The anticipated number of awards is 30, with an anticipated award ceiling of $2,000,000, and the period of performance is 36 months, beginning October 1, 2025. The grant requires a 50% match from non-federal sources and allows requests of up to $2,000 per body-worn camera . The application is a two-step process, with the first step completed and submitted in Grants.gov and the second step submitted in JustGrants.gov, with a submission deadline of November 10, 2025. The second step is the main grant application.

The equipment and personnel costs included in this application are preliminary estimates and are subject to change. Final costs will be determined through the City’s procurement process, including the results of the Request for Proposals (RFP) and the terms of the grant award. Any adjustments to equipment quantities, specifications, or costs necessary to align with actual procurement outcomes or grant funding limitations will be made in compliance with applicable federal and local policies.  BACKGROUND and ANALYSIS: 
 435 W. Portage, LLC, an entity of the Northern Hotels Group (NHG), has submitted an application requesting the establishment of a Commercial Redevelopment District (CRD) under Public Act 255 of 1978. The request pertains to a cluster of parcels located at 435, 437, and 447 West Portage Avenue, as well as two adjacent parcels along W. Portage Avenue. Collectively, these properties comprise the former Karl's Cuisine site within the City’s Central Business District (CBD) and directly adjacent to the Soo Locks—a high-visibility and high-impact location for tourism, hospitality, and downtown activity. 

 NHG is an established hotel development and management group with more than 12 hotels in Michigan, including the Hampton Inn in Sault Ste. Marie and the national award-winning Hampton Inn St. Ignace. Their development history demonstrates the successful delivery of high-quality hospitality facilities with strong operational performance and service standards. 

 The applicant is seeking to clear and redevelop the subject properties to support a two-phase hospitality investment totaling $30 million. 

 Under Act 255, a Commercial Redevelopment District may be established in areas characterized by obsolete or distressed commercial properties in need of rehabilitation or replacement. The former Karl’s Cuisine structures and surrounding site features are currently non-functional, underutilized, and in need of substantial redevelopment. The proposed project meets the statutory requirements by replacing obsolete commercial improvements with modern, high-value hotel facilities. 

 The project advances multiple City and regional economic development objectives: 
 Downtown Revitalization Located in the Central Business District’s primary visitor arrival zone, the project supports ongoing downtown reinvestment and increases year-round economic activity. 

 Tourism Growth With proximity to the Soo Locks—the region’s highest-traffic attraction—the addition of 202 new hotel rooms enhances visitor capacity and positions the city to capture increased tourism demand. 

 Private Investment Leveraging A $30 million investment within the downtown corridor catalyzes further private development and signals investor confidence in Sault Ste. Marie’s economic trajectory. 

 Workforce and Business Support The project’s 40 FTE jobs (average salary $45,000) strengthen the local hospitality workforce, and new lodging options support downtown restaurants, retailers, and attractions. 

 The redevelopment includes full demolition of existing structures and site features, resolving long-standing challenges associated with aging buildings and fragmented parcels. A two
The phase approach provides realistic staging while maintaining momentum for timely completion. 

 BOARDS AND COMMISSION ACTION: 
 Establishing the CRD does not approve incentives by itself; rather, it enables the applicant to pursue a Commercial Rehabilitation Exemption Certificate (CREC) at a later phase. The district creation is a procedural prerequisite that allows the City Commission to evaluate a future abatement request on its merits. Along with a public hearing for the CRD, an additional request for a public hearing for a Commercial Facilities Exemption on January 19 will be added to the agenda.

 1) Motion to amend the TIFA III and Airport Operations FY 2025-26 budgets by $221,800 to purchase a 2025 John Deere 644G Wheel Loader for Sanderson Field Airport.
2) Motion to award the bid to AIS Construction Equipment in the amount of $221,800. 

 BACKGROUND and ANALYSIS: 
 Sanderson Field Airport relies heavily on a wheel loader for winter maintenance operations, particularly for snow removal activities critical to maintaining safe and operational airfield conditions. The airport’s current wheel loader, a 1993 Caterpillar 936F, has reached the end of its reliable service life and is no longer able to safely or effectively support airport operations. 
 The existing loader experiences significant mechanical and safety deficiencies, including inoperable brakes, a damaged flywheel, stress cracks in the loader arms from supporting the airport’s 11,000-pound snow blower, and severely worn pivot points. In addition, extensive rust on operator platforms and grab handles presents increased safety risks. The estimated cost to address these issues exceeds $72,000, yet such repairs would only provide short-term relief and would not resolve the underlying reliability and capacity limitations of the machine. 
 The wheel loader is utilized in over 60% of all snow operations at Sanderson Field, making reliability essential to uninterrupted airport operations during the winter months. Continued downtime or equipment failure directly impacts the airport’s ability to maintain clear runways, taxiways, and aprons, posing safety and operational concerns. 
 To address these issues, airport staff evaluated replacement options, including certified pre-owned equipment and new equipment alternatives. After review, staff recommend the purchase of a new 2025 John Deere 644G wheel loader through AIS Construction Equipment, which offers the best combination of operational fit, long-term value, and risk mitigation. 
 The recommended 2025 John Deere 644G wheel loader provides sufficient horsepower, weight, and structural capacity to safely operate the airport’s existing snow blower and attachments. The proposed purchase takes advantage of substantial government and manufacturer discounts, resulting in a final purchase price of $221,800, including a 5-year extended warranty and attachment bracket. This pricing includes delivery, snow tires, a coupler, a bucket, and a 1-year factory warranty. 
 While lower-cost used options were reviewed, including a 2018 Volvo L110H and a used 2024 John Deere 644G, both alternatives present increased risk due to limited maintenance history, lack of certification, and reduced compatibility with existing in-house maintenance capabilities. Rental-use equipment, in particular, raises concerns regarding long-term durability and the likelihood of major repairs within 5–10 years. Additionally, the City currently stocks parts and has mechanical experience with John Deere equipment, further supporting the recommended option. 
 The proposed budget amendment to the TIFA III budget will allow for the acquisition of this critical piece of infrastructure equipment. Investment in a new wheel loader is anticipated to provide up to 30 years of service life, aligning with long-term capital planning objectives while reducing maintenance costs, improving operational reliability, and enhancing safety for airport staff and users. 
 Approval of the budget amendment will ensure Sanderson Field Airport maintains reliable winter operations, protects public safety, and avoids escalating maintenance expenses associated with continued use of obsolete equipment. 
 BOARDS AND COMMISSION ACTION: 
 At the December 9th, 2025, TIFA III Board Meeting, the board moved to post an RFP for a new or used Wheel Loader. The RFP was then posted, and three bids were received. At the January 13th, 2026, TIFA III board meeting, the TIFA III board unanimously moved for a budget amendment and to award the bid to AIS Construction Equipment based on a recommendation from the Airport Manager and the DPW Director. 
 FISCAL IMPACT: 
 A budget amendment of $221,800 is needed in GL 247-965-965-581 to transfer funds from TIFA III to the Airport for this purchase. The current TIFA III fund balance is sufficient to support the purchase of this piece of equipment with a budgeted 6/30/2026 fund balance of $717,000. 
 A budget amendment of $221,800 is needed within the Airport Fund in GL 581-000-699.247 to record the transfer in from TIFA III as well as an increase in GL 581-902-977.000 in the amount of $221,800 to record the purchase of the equipment. 
 Additionally, Stock and Equipment will receive a $15,000 trade-in offer for the current wheel loader as the original purchaser of the 1993 wheel loader. 
 ALTERNATIVES:

 The City Commission has the following options to consider on this matter:

 Direct staff to return with more information. 
 Other Alternative 
 Take no action. 
 Staff Instructions for Payment Processing: 
 If approved, this will provide documentation for a new PO, payable to AIS Construction in the amount of $221,800 and charged to 581-902-977.000.

 BACKGROUND AND ANALYSIS: 
 The Police Department is undertaking a larger project to replace aging in-car, body-worn, and interview room camera systems. Equipment purchased in 2016 has exceeded its expected life cycle and is experiencing increasing malfunctions and discontinued manufacturer support. The City released a Request for Proposals (RFP) on September 18, 2025, to identify a vendor capable of providing a modern, integrated camera system. 

 This agenda item addresses only the body-worn camera portion of that larger replacement project. The in-car and interview room camera components are separate and are not included in the grant request or cost figures outlined below. 

 The body-worn camera component includes the replacement of existing units and expansion to additional personnel through the purchase of 15 new cameras and supporting infrastructure. A modern system will provide reliable video capture and storage, automated redaction and transcription capabilities, secure digital evidence management, and efficient evidence sharing with the Prosecutor’s Office and partner agencies, improving transparency, accountability, and operational efficiency. 

 To support this portion of the project, the Department seeks to apply for funding through the Small, Rural, and Tribal Body-Worn Camera Program (SRT BWC). This federal micro-grant program supports small and rural law enforcement agencies in implementing or expanding comprehensive body-worn camera programs. The program requires a 1:1 cash or in-kind match and allows up to $2,000 per body-worn camera. Funds must support new or expanded BWC programs and may not reimburse previously purchased equipment. 

 The application is submitted through an online portal and consists of two components: a program application and a detailed budget with budget narrative. Submission of both components constitutes Phase 1 of the grant process, after which eligible applications advance to competitive review. 

 Drafts of the application and budget are attached to this agenda item for Commission review. If approved, the Chief of Police will submit both components electronically through the SRT BWC web portal prior to the deadline. 

 Current estimated costs for the body-worn camera portion of the project are $52,772. These costs include body-worn cameras, mounting equipment, docking and charging stations, Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) evidence management, support software (including redaction and transcription tools), software programming, maintenance and upgrade fees, shipping, and professional services. These items support secure evidence storage, automated uploads, policy-compliant evidence sharing, system configuration, and long-term sustainability. 

 If awarded, the grant will support implementation of a comprehensive body-worn camera program consistent with federal best practices. This request does not include funding for in-car or interview room camera equipment. 

 FISCAL IMPACT: 
 The Department is currently requesting an estimated $26,386 in federal funding with a required estimated $26,386 non-federal match, for a current total estimated project cost of $52,772. These amounts apply only to the body-worn camera component of the larger camera replacement project. 

 All costs are preliminary estimates based on current pricing and projected needs. Final costs will be determined through the City’s procurement process and the terms of any grant award and may increase or decrease accordingly. Any resulting contract for the body-worn camera component will be brought before the City Commission for review and approval in accordance with City purchasing policies. 
 As no vendor has been formally selected and the project remains in the procurement phase, no budget amendment is requested at this time; grant application only.

 BACKGROUND and ANALYSIS: 
 The City purchases bulk gasoline and diesel fuel for the operation of its municipal fleet and equipment, including vehicles utilized by the Department of Public Works, Parks and Recreation, Marina, and other City departments. Approximately 85% of the City's bulk fuel purchases are for Kemp Marina, with the associated costs recovered through revenue generated from marina fuel sales. Historically, the City purchases between 45,000 and 50,000 gallons of bulk fuel annually, although actual quantities vary based on operational needs, marina fuel sales, and market conditions. 

 Rather than soliciting separate competitive bids, staff recommends utilizing the State of Michigan's MiDEAL Extended Purchasing Program. MiDEAL is a cooperative purchasing program administered by the Michigan Department of Technology, Management and Budget (DTMB) that allows local units of government to purchase goods and services through competitively bid State contracts. Utilizing the MiDEAL program provides competitive pricing, reduces administrative effort, and satisfies the City's procurement requirements. 

 The current MiDEAL contract for bulk gasoline and diesel fuel delivery in the Lower Peninsula and Eastern Upper Peninsula has been awarded to Crystal Flash under State Contract No. 250000001316, which is effective through September 30, 2028. 

 Staff also recommends continuing to utilize Autore Oil & Propane Co. for bulk fuel purchases. Autore has supplied bulk fuel to Kemp Marina for more than 10 years and, while not considered a local vendor under the City's purchasing policy, is the nearest bulk fuel supplier serving the area. Their familiarity with the City's fueling operations and proximity make them a reliable source for timely deliveries. 

 It is the intent of staff to obtain pricing from both Crystal Flash and Autore Oil & Propane Co. at the time fuel deliveries are needed and purchase from the supplier offering the best value. Authorizing purchases from both vendors will provide pricing flexibility, improve supply reliability, and ensure continuity of fuel deliveries throughout the fiscal year. 

 Approval of this authorization will not limit the City's ability to purchase fuel from other vendors should operational needs, emergency situations, or supply disruptions warrant doing so. 

 Staff recommends authorizing the purchase of bulk gasoline and diesel fuel through both the MiDEAL contract with Crystal Flash and Autore Oil & Propane Co. for the City's fuel requirements during the FY 2026-27 fiscal year. 

 FISCAL IMPACT: 
 Bulk fuel purchases are budgeted annually within the operating budgets of the various City departments. Actual expenditures fluctuate based on fuel market prices and annual fuel consumption. 

 Approximately 85% of bulk fuel purchased by the City is sold through Kemp Marina. The cost of this fuel is recovered through marina fuel sales, with the remaining fuel utilized for municipal fleet and equipment operations. 

 Purchases made from either authorized supplier will be charged to the appropriate departmental fuel accounts as incurred. Utilizing the MiDEAL contract provides competitively procured pricing without requiring the City to conduct its own bid process. Historically, Autore Oil & Propane Co. has been approved as a sole-source provider for bulk fuel purchases due to its proximity and ability to reliably service the City's fueling needs. 

 Authorizing both suppliers will allow staff to compare pricing at the time each delivery is required and purchase fuel from the vendor offering the most advantageous price while maintaining flexibility and ensuring an uninterrupted fuel supply. 

 No budget amendment is requested or required.

Agenda Item Details 

 Meeting 
 Aug 17, 2026 - Regular City Commission Meeting 
 Category 
 E. SPECIAL ORDERS OF BUSINESS 
 Subject 
 1. Public Hearing and First Reading of an Ordinance to Establish a Planned Unit Development at 1200 Ryan Avenue, the former Washington Elementary School, and Schedule a Second Reading for the September 8, 2026, City Commission meeting a)Hold the Public Hearing b)Take Action on the Request 
 Type 
 Action 
 Preferred Date 
 Aug 17, 2026 
 Absolute Date 
 Aug 17, 2026 
 Fiscal Impact 
 No 
 Recommended Action 
 Motion to concur with the Planning Commission's recommendation and schedule a second reading for the proposed PUD for the September 8th, 2026 City Commission meeting. 

 BACKGROUND: 
 An application ( ATTACHMENT I ) has been submitted by Sidock Group, on behalf of Cloverland Electric Cooperative to rezone the property located at 1200 Ryan Avenue, formerly known as Washington Elementary School, from One-Family Residential to Planning Unit Development. An aerial photograph is included as ATTACHMENT II . 

 The subject property is comprised of a single approximately 7.22-acre unplatted parcel containing an approximately 28,000 square foot single-story former school. The entire property is zoned R-1, which is primarily a one-family zoning district. In addition to single-family dwellings which account for the vast majority of uses in the district, it also permits typical municipal amenities such as parks and libraries, churches established prior to 1965 (the initial date of ordinance adoption), public, parochial, or private elementary schools by right. Other use types permitted subject to conditions include utility facilities serving the immediate vicinity, higher ed institutions, golf courses, and churches established post-1965. 

 As noted previously, the building served as the home of Washington School from its construction in the mid-1950s to the conclusion of the 2024-2025 school year at which point the building was closed. Since closure, Sault Area Public Schools has been seeking parties interested in purchasing the property and building. Given the rather large size of the property and building, there hasn’t been a great deal of interest expressed, particularly in the context of what is permitted by right or subject to conditions in the R-1 district. 

 Cloverland Electric Cooperative has been in discussions regarding the purchase of this property as they’ve been strongly considering utilizing the property as a lineman training facility, available to their employees as well as those of other electrical utilities. Plans additionally include the relocation of a component of their administrative employees from other offices to the school property. 

 The plans presented at the time of application call for the retention of the building as it sits along with the construction of an addition at the rear of the existing building to house an indoor space to do pole work indoors. That space is proposed to be on the order of 10,000 square feet and contain training space, storage, and locker rooms. This addition is proposed at a single roof-pitch with the high side at about 42.5 feet in height and the low side at 32 feet in height. The submitted PUD concept plan documents are included as ATTACHMENT III . 

 This application represents the second to utilize the new PUD regulations which were adopted by the City Commission in mid-2025. At its core, the PUD is a tool designed to provide added flexibility in property development thereby encouraging innovative land use, variety in design, and achieve economy an efficiency in the use of land, among many other things. It is also useful in that the aforementioned flexibility can assist in the redevelopment of sites which exhibit difficult development constraints which is more common with infill sites versus those being developed for the first time. The full PUD ordinance is included as ATTACHMENT IV . 

 Procedurally, this request is treated similarly to a rezoning in that the Planning Commission makes a recommendation to the City Commission whether to approve, deny, or approve with conditions. The City Commission takes that recommendation into consideration when making their own decision. If the City Commission approves the project or approves the project with conditions, the applicant has three years to return to the Planning Commission with a formal site plan review application to wrap up any final details prior to beginning project construction. Provided future phases are consistent with the plans initially approved, a return to the Planning Commission isn’t necessary prior to commencing construction. 

 ANALYSIS: 
 As already noted, this site is zoned R-1, which is a one-family zoning designation. As such, the specific use intended for the property is not permitted. While the PUD regulations do allow a bit of flexibility in the R-1 district by allowing multifamily uses, but nothing beyond such as what is proposed by Cloverland. Additionally, the height of the new addition exceeds the maximum building height of 30 feet so a wavier would need to be granted for the added height as well as the nature of the use proposed. 

 Pursuant to Section 10-1.15C11(b), the Planning Commission and City Commission are authorized to grant waivers to the requirements and standards of the underlying (in this case Tourist) zoning district subject to the following standards, each of which the Planning Commission and City Commission find must be met: 

 The waiver will result in an improvement to the design or function of the building or site which would not be possible following the standards of the zoning district. 

 The need for the waiver cannot be the result of a self-created situation. 

 The waiver cannot be sought to circumvent or avoid the requirements of the zoning ordinance. 

 Given that two waivers are being requested, staff will address compliance with the waiver standards individually. 

 Permitted Use Wavier: 

 From a staff standpoint, former school sites pose significant challenges for reuse as they typically take the form of large buildings in areas which, outside of a rather limited number of complimentary uses, are intended for one-family residential uses. This City’s history in particular has several examples of former school facilities such as the former Jefferson Elementary School and former Garfield Elementary School (now rehabbed into housing) which were at one point or continue to be long-time visual blights in their respective neighborhoods. The PUD process provides an opportunity, under the correct circumstances, of that possibility occurring in this instance. 

 In the opinion of staff, the first waiver condition is met as the reuse of the building would not be possible following standards of the zoning district. The district permits only a small number of uses to occupy the property, none of which are likely to occur there. 

 The need for the use waiver is not self-created, but rather the result of the need to authorize the use at the site. 

 The use waiver is not being sought simply as a means of circumventing or avoiding requirements of the Zoning Ordinance as it is necessary for the project to move forward as envisioned. 

 Height Wavier: 

 As previously stated, the maximum height in the R-1 zoning district is 30 feet. The new training addition is proposed to have a single pitched with a total height of 32 feet at its western wall and 42.5 feet at its eastern wall where it would meet the existing building. The intent of this part of the building is to provide indoor space where poles can be mounted to the floor for training to take place at a height where pole-mounted electrical equipment would typically be installed out in the field. 

 If following the standards of the district, this height would not be achievable, making the waiver necessary to provide for a realistic training environment. 

 There is no self-created hardship aspect to the request for the height waiver. It is necessary to provide training at the height of typical pole-mounted equipment. 

 The request is based upon a legitimate need and not simply as a way to circumvent the requirements of the Zoning Ordinance. 

 Based upon the following standards, the Planning Commission may recommend denial, approval, or approval with conditions, and the City Commission may deny, approve, or approve with conditions the proposed PUD. 

 The uses proposed shall be consistent with the city's adopted Master Plan. Such uses must have a beneficial effect, in terms of public health, safety, welfare, or convenience, on present and future potential surrounding land uses. The uses proposed must not adversely affect the public utility and circulation system, surrounding properties, or the environment. The public benefit shall be one which could not be achieved under the regulations of the underlying district alone or that of any other zoning district. 

 Staff response: The subject property is within the “School Use” future land use designation as it was still an active educational facility when the Master Plan was adopted. The Master Plan offers no specific guidance on what should occur in the event the school use is discontinued other than the importance of coordination and collaboration with the school district regarding their future use and development. 

 Given that the surrounding areas a largely residential there needs to be particular attention given to how the proposed use will interact with its surroundings since it would ordinarily by considered incompatible. Topics such as traffic generation, hours of activity, and the site’s accessory uses are all important to cover. With adequate safeguards and conditions in place, it is the opinion of staff that the proposed use of the site can be one which is beneficial to the neighborhood, particularly in the context of paths taken by other former schools within the City. The proposed use is one which could not be undertaken under the underlying district nor responsibly under any other zoning district. An excerpt of the Future Land Use Map is included as ATTACHMENT V . 

 Any waivers from the requirements or standards of the underlying zoning district or special use(s) in accordance with Section 15C11, Appeals and Variances, such as, but not limited to, density, lot sizes, setbacks, height limits, required facilities, buffers, open space, or permitted sign area, shall be reviewed and approved by the Planning Commission when it is determined that the waivers will accomplish the objectives identified in this section and be consistent with the intent and purpose of the underlying zoning district. 

 Staff response: In any motions made, the Planning Commission and City Commission should specifically address whether or not the requested waivers will accomplish the identified objectives and be consistent with the intent and purpose of the underlying zoning district. 

 The number and dimensions of off-street parking shall be sufficient to meet the minimum required by Section 1704, Parking Requirements. However, where warranted by overlapping or shared parking arrangements, the Planning Commission may grant a waiver reducing the required number of parking spaces. 

 Staff response: The proposed plan shows 28 marked parking spaces along with two large, paved areas which are presumed to be multi-purpose. The Zoning Ordinance requires parking added only when there is new square footage being constructed, therefore, only the new addition requires additional parking spaces to be constructed. There is no category in the Zoning Ordinance for the specific use intended for that space. The closest listed use would be the category including dance halls, roller rinks and assembly halls without fixed seats where a parking requirement of 1 space per 100 square feet of usable area is required. Utilizing that calculation over the approximately 9,000 square feet of training area yields a parking requirement of about 90 spaces. Where a room has a legal capacity established, it needs to be parked at 1 space for every four occupants. Despite the lower number of parking space on-site there appears to be sufficient physical space for them and this matter will be more thoroughly investigated during the site plan approval process should the preliminary PUD plan be approved. No overlapping or shared parking agreements are proposed or requested. 

 All streets and parking areas within the PUD shall meet the minimum construction and other requirements of city ordinances, unless modified by City Commission or Planning Commission, depending upon which body possesses jurisdiction under the City Code. 

 Staff response: No requests to deviate from the minimum construction standards or other requirements have been made by the applicant. 

 Safe, convenient, uncongested, and well-defined vehicular and pedestrian circulation within and to the site shall be provided. Drives, streets, and other elements shall be designed to discourage through traffic, while promoting safe and efficient traffic operations within the site and at its access points. 

 Staff response: Cloverland proposes to retain the existing driveway on Dillon Street, which is considered a local street, as well as add a second driveway on Ryan Avenue on the south side of the existing building, which is considered a major street. With the high likelihood of a non-trivial number of utility trucks accessing the site, staff is concerned about the potential impact to Dillon Street both in terms of accelerated deterioration of the street surface as well as noise and traffic. To address those concerns, staff recommends limiting the driveway on Dillon Street to passenger vehicles only. The Ryan Street driveway would then become the sole point of ingress and egress for utility trucks and similar types of vehicles coming and going from the site. This condition would be accompanied by “No Trucks” signage at either end of Dillon Street or something similar. 

 Sidewalks shall be provided in accordance with the City Complete Streets Resolution dated August 2, 2010. 

 Staff response: The Ryan Street frontage is currently developed with sidewalks as is a portion of the Dillon Street frontage. Additional sidewalk will need to be added along Dillon Street if the requirement is not otherwise waived by the Planning Commission. 

 Landscaping shall be preserved and/or provided to ensure that proposed uses will be adequately buffered from one another and from surrounding public and private property. Plantings and other landscape features shall exceed the standards of Section 1709, Screening, Buffering and Landscaping. 

 Staff response: Detailed landscape plans have not been submitted as part of this application, however, it appears that no existing vegetation is slated for removal outside of the grass in the vicinity of the proposed addition and areas of paving. A more detailed review will be completed at the time of site plan review, however, required landscaping is not shown buffering the new parking areas from public streets nor from the adjoining residential uses, which will be required. 

 The narrative submitted with the application notes that the existing open areas may remain for passive recreation, including the buffer along the west property line. There are currently no buffers maintained along the north or south property lines which directly abut or are across the street from residential uses. The Planning Commission may wish to consider requiring the installation of buffering along the north and south property lines as well as the unbuffered portion of the west property line in anticipation that Cloverland may desire to expand into that space someday. Rather than requiring the installation of the landscaping at the time of expansion, there is some logic to requiring it as part of this application to permit time to grow in so that it will be more effective when its presence becomes necessary. 

 Judicious effort shall be used to preserve significant natural, historical, and architectural features and the integrity of the land, including regulated and nonregulated wetlands. 

 Staff response: The school building itself is a significant historical and architectural feature which will be preserved should this project obtain required approvals. There are no regulated or nonregulated wetlands on the property. 

 Surface water shall be retained on the site wherever possible. 

 Staff response: The applicant is proposing a detention basin along the west line of the property to collect and contain surface runoff. It is proposed to be connected to the stormwater collection system on Dillon Street. 

 The site shall have adequate lateral support so as to ensure that there will be no erosion of soil or other material. The final determination as to adequacy of, or need for, lateral support shall be made by the City Engineer. 

 Staff response: Staff is confident that no issues with arise in this regard. During the site plan review process, the City’s Engineering Department is part of the review team and will become more involved at that time. 

 Public water and sewer facilities shall be available or shall be provided by the developer as part of the site development. 

 Staff response: Public water and sewer facilities are available and with sufficient capacity to serve the proposed development. 

 Building design shall be of a high quality and exceed the design requirements of the zoning ordinance. 

 Staff response: The school’s design will remain unchanged with the exception of the rear addition for the training facility and ancillary spaces. 

 BOARDS AND COMMISSION ACTION: 
 The Planning Commission considered this request at their July 23, 2026, meeting and unanimously recommended that the request be approved with the following conditions: 

 1. Truck traffic exiting from the site's driveway onto Dillon Street shall be limited to right turns only to reach Ryan Avenue. The applicant shall install at its expense and to the satisfaction of the City Engineer "No Trucks" signs at the west end of Dillon Street at is its intersection with Meridian Street as well as on the west side of the site's Dillon Street driveway. 

 2. No equipment aside from that necessary to serve the immediate needs of the site shall be permitted to be placed or installed on-site. Any backup generator installed on the site shall be located within a sound-reducing enclosure and screened from adjoining property or a building adequate for the same purpose. 

 In making their recommendation, the Planning Commission additionally found as follows: 

 That the application met the qualifying conditions including 1,4, and 5 in 15C02(a). 
 The requested use and height waivers met the conditions for approval in 15C11 and accomplish identified objectives. 
 The presented PUD plan met approval standards in 15C05. 
 The sidewalk requirement along Dillon Street between the north driveway and west property line should be waived. 
 The PUD should be approved subject to conditions one and two noted above. 

 Prior to the Planning Commission meeting, staff received public feedback expressing concerns from a resident about the loss of playground facilities, impacts on Dillon Street, and the long-term use of the outdoor space west of the building. No public comment was received at the meeting itself. As part of its report and recommendation to the Planning Commission, staff suggested conditions beyond what was ultimately recommended by the Planning Commission. The staff report provided to the Planning Commission is included as ATTACHMENT VI . 

 FISCAL IMPACT: 
 Although there is no direct fiscal impact from the PUD rezoning request itself, the transition of this property from public ownership to private will result in it going on the tax rolls.
