5) Motion to approve the overall PUD plan subject to the Planning Commission-recommended conditions pertaining to the Dillon Street driveway and outside placement of items and equipment. 

 BACKGROUND: 
 An application ( ATTACHMENT I ) has been submitted by Sidock Group, on behalf of Cloverland Electric Cooperative to rezone the property located at 1200 Ryan Avenue, formerly known as Washington Elementary School, from One-Family Residential to Planning Unit Development. An aerial photograph is included as ATTACHMENT II . 

 The subject property is comprised of a single approximately 7.22-acre unplatted parcel containing an approximately 28,000 square foot single-story former school. The entire property is zoned R-1, which is primarily a one-family zoning district. In addition to single-family dwellings which account for the vast majority of uses in the district, it also permits typical municipal amenities such as parks and libraries, churches established prior to 1965 (the initial date of ordinance adoption), public, parochial, or private elementary schools by right. Other use types permitted subject to conditions include utility facilities serving the immediate vicinity, higher ed institutions, golf courses, and churches established post-1965. 

 As noted previously, the building served as the home of Washington School from its construction in the mid-1950s to the conclusion of the 2024-2025 school year at which point the building was closed. Since closure, Sault Area Public Schools has been seeking parties interested in purchasing the property and building. Given the rather large size of the property and building, there hasn’t been a great deal of interest expressed, particularly in the context of what is permitted by right or subject to conditions in the R-1 district. 

 Cloverland Electric Cooperative has been in discussions regarding the purchase of this property as they’ve been strongly considering utilizing the property as a lineman training facility, available to their employees as well as those of other electrical utilities. Plans additionally include the relocation of a component of their administrative employees from other offices to the school property. 

 The plans presented at the time of application call for the retention of the building as it sits along with the construction of an addition at the rear of the existing building to house an indoor space to do pole work indoors. That space is proposed to be on the order of 10,000 square feet and contain training space, storage, and locker rooms. This addition is proposed at a single roof-pitch with the high side at about 42.5 feet in height and the low side at 32 feet in height. The submitted PUD concept plan documents are included as ATTACHMENT III . 

 This application represents the second to utilize the new PUD regulations which were adopted by the City Commission in mid-2025. At its core, the PUD is a tool designed to provide added flexibility in property development thereby encouraging innovative land use, variety in design, and achieve economy an efficiency in the use of land, among many other things. It is also useful in that the aforementioned flexibility can assist in the redevelopment of sites which exhibit difficult development constraints which is more common with infill sites versus those being developed for the first time. The full PUD ordinance is included as ATTACHMENT IV . 

 Procedurally, this request is treated similarly to a rezoning in that the Planning Commission makes a recommendation to the City Commission whether to approve, deny, or approve with conditions. The City Commission takes that recommendation into consideration when making their own decision. If the City Commission approves the project or approves the project with conditions, the applicant has three years to return to the Planning Commission with a formal site plan review application to wrap up any final details prior to beginning project construction. Provided future phases are consistent with the plans initially approved, a return to the Planning Commission isn’t necessary prior to commencing construction. 

 ANALYSIS: 
 As already noted, this site is zoned R-1, which is a one-family zoning designation. As such, the specific use intended for the property is not permitted. While the PUD regulations do allow a bit of flexibility in the R-1 district by allowing multifamily uses, but nothing beyond such as what is proposed by Cloverland. Additionally, the height of the new addition exceeds the maximum building height of 30 feet so a wavier would need to be granted for the added height as well as the nature of the use proposed. 

 Pursuant to Section 10-1.15C11(b), the Planning Commission and City Commission are authorized to grant waivers to the requirements and standards of the underlying (in this case Tourist) zoning district subject to the following standards, each of which the Planning Commission and City Commission find must be met: 

 The waiver will result in an improvement to the design or function of the building or site which would not be possible following the standards of the zoning district. 

 The need for the waiver cannot be the result of a self-created situation. 

 The waiver cannot be sought to circumvent or avoid the requirements of the zoning ordinance. 

 Given that two waivers are being requested, staff will address compliance with the waiver standards individually. 

 Permitted Use Wavier: 

 From a staff standpoint, former school sites pose significant challenges for reuse as they typically take the form of large buildings in areas which, outside of a rather limited number of complimentary uses, are intended for one-family residential uses. This City’s history in particular has several examples of former school facilities such as the former Jefferson Elementary School and former Garfield Elementary School (now rehabbed into housing) which were at one point or continue to be long-time visual blights in their respective neighborhoods. The PUD process provides an opportunity, under the correct circumstances, of that possibility occurring in this instance. 

 In the opinion of staff, the first waiver condition is met as the reuse of the building would not be possible following standards of the zoning district. The district permits only a small number of uses to occupy the property, none of which are likely to occur there. 

 The need for the use waiver is not self-created, but rather the result of the need to authorize the use at the site. 

 The use waiver is not being sought simply as a means of circumventing or avoiding requirements of the Zoning Ordinance as it is necessary for the project to move forward as envisioned. 

 Height Wavier: 

 As previously stated, the maximum height in the R-1 zoning district is 30 feet. The new training addition is proposed to have a single pitched with a total height of 32 feet at its western wall and 42.5 feet at its eastern wall where it would meet the existing building. The intent of this part of the building is to provide indoor space where poles can be mounted to the floor for training to take place at a height where pole-mounted electrical equipment would typically be installed out in the field. 

 If following the standards of the district, this height would not be achievable, making the waiver necessary to provide for a realistic training environment. 

 There is no self-created hardship aspect to the request for the height waiver. It is necessary to provide training at the height of typical pole-mounted equipment. 

 The request is based upon a legitimate need and not simply as a way to circumvent the requirements of the Zoning Ordinance. 

 Based upon the following standards, the Planning Commission may recommend denial, approval, or approval with conditions, and the City Commission may deny, approve, or approve with conditions the proposed PUD. 

 The uses proposed shall be consistent with the city's adopted Master Plan. Such uses must have a beneficial effect, in terms of public health, safety, welfare, or convenience, on present and future potential surrounding land uses. The uses proposed must not adversely affect the public utility and circulation system, surrounding properties, or the environment. The public benefit shall be one which could not be achieved under the regulations of the underlying district alone or that of any other zoning district. 

 Staff response: The subject property is within the “School Use” future land use designation as it was still an active educational facility when the Master Plan was adopted. The Master Plan offers no specific guidance on what should occur in the event the school use is discontinued other than the importance of coordination and collaboration with the school district regarding their future use and development. 

 Given that the surrounding areas a largely residential there needs to be particular attention given to how the proposed use will interact with its surroundings since it would ordinarily by considered incompatible. Topics such as traffic generation, hours of activity, and the site’s accessory uses are all important to cover. With adequate safeguards and conditions in place, it is the opinion of staff that the proposed use of the site can be one which is beneficial to the neighborhood, particularly in the context of paths taken by other former schools within the City. The proposed use is one which could not be undertaken under the underlying district nor responsibly under any other zoning district. An excerpt of the Future Land Use Map is included as ATTACHMENT V . 

 Any waivers from the requirements or standards of the underlying zoning district or special use(s) in accordance with Section 15C11, Appeals and Variances, such as, but not limited to, density, lot sizes, setbacks, height limits, required facilities, buffers, open space, or permitted sign area, shall be reviewed and approved by the Planning Commission when it is determined that the waivers will accomplish the objectives identified in this section and be consistent with the intent and purpose of the underlying zoning district. 

 Staff response: In any motions made, the Planning Commission and City Commission should specifically address whether or not the requested waivers will accomplish the identified objectives and be consistent with the intent and purpose of the underlying zoning district. 

 The number and dimensions of off-street parking shall be sufficient to meet the minimum required by Section 1704, Parking Requirements. However, where warranted by overlapping or shared parking arrangements, the Planning Commission may grant a waiver reducing the required number of parking spaces. 

 Staff response: The proposed plan shows 28 marked parking spaces along with two large, paved areas which are presumed to be multi-purpose. The Zoning Ordinance requires parking added only when there is new square footage being constructed, therefore, only the new addition requires additional parking spaces to be constructed. There is no category in the Zoning Ordinance for the specific use intended for that space. The closest listed use would be the category including dance halls, roller rinks and assembly halls without fixed seats where a parking requirement of 1 space per 100 square feet of usable area is required. Utilizing that calculation over the approximately 9,000 square feet of training area yields a parking requirement of about 90 spaces. Where a room has a legal capacity established, it needs to be parked at 1 space for every four occupants. Despite the lower number of parking space on-site there appears to be sufficient physical space for them and this matter will be more thoroughly investigated during the site plan approval process should the preliminary PUD plan be approved. No overlapping or shared parking agreements are proposed or requested. 

 All streets and parking areas within the PUD shall meet the minimum construction and other requirements of city ordinances, unless modified by City Commission or Planning Commission, depending upon which body possesses jurisdiction under the City Code. 

 Staff response: No requests to deviate from the minimum construction standards or other requirements have been made by the applicant. 

 Safe, convenient, uncongested, and well-defined vehicular and pedestrian circulation within and to the site shall be provided. Drives, streets, and other elements shall be designed to discourage through traffic, while promoting safe and efficient traffic operations within the site and at its access points. 

 Staff response: Cloverland proposes to retain the existing driveway on Dillon Street, which is considered a local street, as well as add a second driveway on Ryan Avenue on the south side of the existing building, which is considered a major street. With the high likelihood of a non-trivial number of utility trucks accessing the site, staff is concerned about the potential impact to Dillon Street both in terms of accelerated deterioration of the street surface as well as noise and traffic. To address those concerns, staff recommends limiting the driveway on Dillon Street to passenger vehicles only. The Ryan Street driveway would then become the sole point of ingress and egress for utility trucks and similar types of vehicles coming and going from the site. This condition would be accompanied by “No Trucks” signage at either end of Dillon Street or something similar. 

 Sidewalks shall be provided in accordance with the City Complete Streets Resolution dated August 2, 2010. 

 Staff response: The Ryan Street frontage is currently developed with sidewalks as is a portion of the Dillon Street frontage. Additional sidewalk will need to be added along Dillon Street if the requirement is not otherwise waived by the Planning Commission. 

 Landscaping shall be preserved and/or provided to ensure that proposed uses will be adequately buffered from one another and from surrounding public and private property. Plantings and other landscape features shall exceed the standards of Section 1709, Screening, Buffering and Landscaping. 

 Staff response: Detailed landscape plans have not been submitted as part of this application, however, it appears that no existing vegetation is slated for removal outside of the grass in the vicinity of the proposed addition and areas of paving. A more detailed review will be completed at the time of site plan review, however, required landscaping is not shown buffering the new parking areas from public streets nor from the adjoining residential uses, which will be required. 

 The narrative submitted with the application notes that the existing open areas may remain for passive recreation, including the buffer along the west property line. There are currently no buffers maintained along the north or south property lines which directly abut or are across the street from residential uses. The Planning Commission may wish to consider requiring the installation of buffering along the north and south property lines as well as the unbuffered portion of the west property line in anticipation that Cloverland may desire to expand into that space someday. Rather than requiring the installation of the landscaping at the time of expansion, there is some logic to requiring it as part of this application to permit time to grow in so that it will be more effective when its presence becomes necessary. 

 Judicious effort shall be used to preserve significant natural, historical, and architectural features and the integrity of the land, including regulated and nonregulated wetlands. 

 Staff response: The school building itself is a significant historical and architectural feature which will be preserved should this project obtain required approvals. There are no regulated or nonregulated wetlands on the property. 

 Surface water shall be retained on the site wherever possible. 

 Staff response: The applicant is proposing a detention basin along the west line of the property to collect and contain surface runoff. It is proposed to be connected to the stormwater collection system on Dillon Street. 

 The site shall have adequate lateral support so as to ensure that there will be no erosion of soil or other material. The final determination as to adequacy of, or need for, lateral support shall be made by the City Engineer. 

 Staff response: Staff is confident that no issues with arise in this regard. During the site plan review process, the City’s Engineering Department is part of the review team and will become more involved at that time. 

 Public water and sewer facilities shall be available or shall be provided by the developer as part of the site development. 

 Staff response: Public water and sewer facilities are available and with sufficient capacity to serve the proposed development. 

 Building design shall be of a high quality and exceed the design requirements of the zoning ordinance. 

 Staff response: The school’s design will remain unchanged with the exception of the rear addition for the training facility and ancillary spaces. 

 BOARDS AND COMMISSION ACTION: 
 The Planning Commission considered this request at their July 23, 2026, meeting and unanimously recommended that the request be approved with the following conditions: 

 1. Truck traffic exiting from the site's driveway onto Dillon Street shall be limited to right turns only to reach Ryan Avenue. The applicant shall install at its expense and to the satisfaction of the City Engineer "No Trucks" signs at the west end of Dillon Street at is its intersection with Meridian Street as well as on the west side of the site's Dillon Street driveway. 

 2. No equipment aside from that necessary to serve the immediate needs of the site shall be permitted to be placed or installed on-site. Any backup generator installed on the site shall be located within a sound-reducing enclosure and screened from adjoining property or a building adequate for the same purpose. 

 In making their recommendation, the Planning Commission additionally found as follows: 

 That the application met the qualifying conditions including 1,4, and 5 in 15C02(a). 
 The requested use and height waivers met the conditions for approval in 15C11 and accomplish identified objectives. 
 The presented PUD plan met approval standards in 15C05. 
 The sidewalk requirement along Dillon Street between the north driveway and west property line should be waived. 
 The PUD should be approved subject to conditions one and two noted above. 

 Prior to the Planning Commission meeting, staff received public feedback expressing concerns from a resident about the loss of playground facilities, impacts on Dillon Street, and the long-term use of the outdoor space west of the building. No public comment was received at the meeting itself. As part of its report and recommendation to the Planning Commission, staff suggested conditions beyond what was ultimately recommended by the Planning Commission. The staff report provided to the Planning Commission is included as ATTACHMENT VI . 

 FISCAL IMPACT: 
 Although there is no direct fiscal impact from the PUD rezoning request itself, the transition of this property from public ownership to private will result in it going on the tax rolls. 

 ALTERNATIVES: 
 List alternatives to the recommended action. 

 The City Commission has the following options to consider on this matter: 
 Adopt the ordinance with modifications. 
 Direct staff to return with more information. 
 Other Alternative 
 Take no action. 

 Motion & Voting 

 1) Motion to find that the Preliminary PUD plan meets the qualifying conditions, including 1, 4, and, 5 in 15C02(a).

Motion by Jodi Bosbous-Rath, second by Scott Marble.

 Final Resolution: Motion Carried

 Yea: Don Gerrie, Ray Bauer, Jodi Bosbous-Rath, Steve Habusta, Scott Marble, Andrew Rubinstein, Tim Talentino

 2) Motion to find that the requested use and height waivers meet the conditions for approval in 15C11 and accomplish identified objectives.

Motion by Jodi Bosbous-Rath, second by Scott Marble.

 Final Resolution: Motion Carried

 Yea: Don Gerrie, Ray Bauer, Jodi Bosbous-Rath, Steve Habusta, Scott Marble, Andrew Rubinstein, Tim Talentino

 3) Motion to find that the Preliminary PUD Plan meets the standards for approval in 15C05.

Motion by Jodi Bosbous-Rath, second by Scott Marble.

 Final Resolution: Motion Carried

 Yea: Don Gerrie, Ray Bauer, Jodi Bosbous-Rath, Steve Habusta, Scott Marble, Andrew Rubinstein, Tim Talentino

 4) Motion to waive the new sidewalk requirement along Dillon Street.

Motion by Jodi Bosbous-Rath, second by Scott Marble.

 Final Resolution: Motion Carried

 Yea: Don Gerrie, Ray Bauer, Jodi Bosbous-Rath, Steve Habusta, Scott Marble, Andrew Rubinstein, Tim Talentino

 5) Motion to approve the overall PUD plan subject to the Planning Commission-recommended conditions pertaining to the Dillon Street driveway and outside placement of items and equipment.

Motion by Jodi Bosbous-Rath, second by Scott Marble.

 Final Resolution: Motion Carried

 Yea: Don Gerrie, Ray Bauer, Jodi Bosbous-Rath, Steve Habusta, Scott Marble, Andrew Rubinstein, Tim Talentino

 Category 
 E. SPECIAL ORDERS OF BUSINESS 
 Subject 
 4. Public Hearing and First Reading of an Ordinance to Establish a Planned Unit Development at 810 East 5th Avenue, the former Lincoln Elementary School, and Schedule a Second Reading for the October 5, 2026, City Commission meeting a) Hold the Public Hearing b) Take Action on the Request

 Fiscal Impact 
 No 
 Recommended Action 
 Staff has included motion pages for the use of the City Commission, one for approval, and one for denial. Select and read the appropriate page for the desired outcome. 

 BACKGROUND: 

 An application ( ATTACHMENT I ) has been submitted by Joshua Billington, on behalf of Lincoln Square Partners, LLC, to rezone the property located at 810 East 5 th Avenue, formerly known as Lincoln Elementary School from One-Family Residential to Planned Unit Development. An aerial photograph is included as ATTACHMENT II . 

 The subject property is composed of three adjoining parcels totaling approximately 7.4-acres. The school building, which is on the order of 43,000 square feet, is located on the north half of the site while the south half of the site contains playgrounds and other outdoor recreational spaces. There are approximately 50 platted lots within the boundary of the site along with numerous vacated streets and alleys. 

 Lincoln School was constructed at this site beginning in 1950 and served the community until its closure at the end of the 2024-2025 school year. Since that time, Sault Area Public Schools has been seeking parties interested in repurposing the property. 

 Today’s Lincoln School was built to replace a previous Lincoln School which stood on the site now occupied by the two blocks north and south of Lincoln Way. That school was in service from around 1900 until it was demolished and the site sold for housing development in 1954. 

 The applicant has been to the Planning Commission twice previously to present plan concepts, both of which involved the reuse of the existing school building, however, those plans were ultimately not feasible given the considerable size and needs of the building. Ultimately, the applicant found that the most economical path is to remove the building from the property. 

 The applicant also hosted a public open house earlier in the summer to solicit feedback from the neighborhood, which was well-attended. The feedback received informed some of the changes seen on the plan accompanying this application. 

 Aside from the removal of the existing building from the property, another significant change proposed is the inclusion of a nearly 2-acre green space in the center of the property which will be available for public enjoyment. Though the exact layout of amenities within the green space is still being solidified, it is the intention of the applicant to retain and reinstall some of the existing playground equipment where reuse is possible. 

 The development itself is planned to take place around the periphery of the green space. The new plan calls for the construction of 18 single-family dwellings (down from 22 originally proposed) and 22 multi-family units (up from 20 originally proposed). A 5,000 square foot senior center and corresponding parking lot are proposed west of the multi-family units. As the senior center plan is still being vetted, the applicant is requesting favorable consideration of an alternate plan which would see the space dedicated to the senior center and parking lot be utilized for the construction of an additional nine units of multiple-family housing. 

 The submitted PUD concept plan documents are included as ATTACHMENT III . The first document shows the plan with the inclusion of the senior center and the second with the expanded multiple-family option. 

 This application represents the third to utilize the new PUD regulations which were adopted by the City Commission in mid-2025. At its core, the PUD is a tool designed to provide added flexibility in property development thereby encouraging innovative land use, variety in design, and achieve economy and efficiency in the use of land, among many other things. It is also useful in that the flexibility can assist in the redevelopment of sites which exhibit difficult development constraints which is more common with infill sites versus those being developed for the first time. The full PUD ordinance is included as ATTACHMENT IV . 

 Procedurally, this request is treated similarly to a rezoning in that the Planning Commission makes a recommendation to the City Commission whether to approve, deny, or approve with conditions. The City Commission takes that recommendation into consideration when making their own decision. If the City Commission approves the project or approves the project with conditions, the applicant has three years to return to the Planning Commission with a formal site plan review application to wrap up any final details prior to beginning project construction. Provided future phases are consistent with the plans initially approved, a return to the Planning Commission isn’t necessary prior to commencing construction. 

 ANALYSIS: 

 The entire site is zoned R-1, a principally one-family zoning designation. The use of permitted uses is quite small and is generally limited to single-family dwellings, public libraries and recreational facilities, municipal buildings and uses, churches (established pre-1965), and public, parochial/other private pre-school or elementary schools. Additional uses such as utility and public services facilities (without storage yards), colleges and universities, golf courses, secondary schools, and churches are additionally permitted subject to special conditions. 

 While one-family and multiple-family uses are anticipated by the PUD regulations, the senior center component of the project is not, so a waiver will be required to permit that part of the project to move forward. All other parts of the project remain in keeping with what is anticipated by the PUD ordinance. As noted previously, the initial concept plans which retained the existing school building were intended to program it as a possible senior center and head start facility operated by an outside agency or provider. At the time, that was the logical choice given the demand for those services in the local area and the need to identify a viable use for such a large building. In the wake of the pivot in plans, the applicant still desires to provide some service component to the site even though the school building is no longer part of the redevelopment strategy. As the senior center would be operated by an outside agency and no specific agreements are in place, the applicant is requesting the ability to utilize that space to expand the number of multi-family units by nine for a total multi-family unit count of 31 and an overall unit count of 49. 

 Pursuant to Section 10-1.15C11(b), the Planning Commission and City Commission are authorized to grant waivers to the requirements and standards of the underlying (in this case R-1) zoning district subject to the following standards, each of which the Planning Commission and City Commission find must be met: 

 The waiver will result in an improvement to the design or function of the building or site which would not be possible following the standards of the zoning district. 

 The need for the waiver cannot be the result of a self-created situation. 

 The waiver cannot be sought to circumvent or avoid the requirements of the zoning ordinance. 

 The idea for the senior center was initially conceived as an adaptive reuse of the school building, which is too large not economical to use for residential purposes. Even though the applicant is no longer considering retaining the school building, the senior center component is desired to be retained, but in a new purpose-built structure and rented out or sold to an entity which would then provide the services. 

 The inclusion of the senior center component would improve the function of the site since it would provide a service that is not readily available in the community. With its location in a residential area such as proposed, the facility would open opportunities for users to walk to the site from home rather than depending upon driving. The facility would also give greater purpose to the sidewalks which were installed shortly before the closure of the school. 

 The need for the waiver isn’t a self-created but instead arises from the desire to retain the community service component which had been part of the original concept plan. Further, the waiver isn’t being requested simply as a means to circumvent the requirements of the ordinance. 

 Were the applicant to go the route of utilizing the land area for additional multiple-family housing, this waiver would not be required. 

 As noted previously, one-family and multiple-family housing is anticipated for PUDs created in the R-1 zoning district. The proposed one-family dwelling sites meet or exceed the minimum standards and dimensional requirements for that type of use, so no waivers are needed. There are no specifically stated standards for the multiple-family component, however, both design concepts comply with the R-1 setback requirements and fall below the maximum permitted density in both the RM-1 and RM-2 districts. 

 During the staff review, it was noted that the two northern-most single-family dwellings on the Superior St side are shown occupying an unvacated right-of-way. The applicant is aware they’ll need to take measures to resolve that matter prior to the approval of the Final PUD plan. 

 Based upon the following standards, the Planning Commission may recommend denial, approval, or approval with conditions, and the City Commission may deny, approve, or approve with conditions the proposed PUD. 

 The uses proposed shall be consistent with the city's adopted Master Plan. Such uses must have a beneficial effect, in terms of public health, safety, welfare, or convenience, on present and future potential surrounding land uses. The uses proposed must not adversely affect the public utility and circulation system, surrounding properties, or the environment. The public benefit shall be one which could not be achieved under the regulations of the underlying district alone or that of any other zoning district. 

 Staff response: The subject property is within the “School Use” future land use designation as it was still an active educational facility when the Master Plan was adopted. The Master Plan offers no specific guidance on what should occur in the event the school use is discontinued other than the importance of coordination and collaboration with the school district regarding their future use and development. 

 The proposed PUD is substantially residential in nature and includes a one-family residential component which is consistent with the existing uses in the area. The multiple-family residential component is permissible in the R-1 district under the terms of the PUD enabling ordinance. The proposed senior center component is likely to be a positive addition to the neighborhood and an unlikely source of negative impacts despite the need for a waiver for its inclusion. 

 Although the Future Land Use Map designates the property as School Use, staff finds the proposed redevelopment compatible with the predominantly residential character of the surrounding neighborhood and consistent with broader Master Plan goals encouraging reinvestment and productive reuse of developed land. 

 An excerpt of the Future Land Use Map is included as ATTACHMENT V . 

 Any waivers from the requirements or standards of the underlying zoning district or special use(s) in accordance with Section 10-1.15C11, Appeals and Variances, such as, but not limited to, density, lot sizes, setbacks, height limits, required facilities, buffers, open space, or permitted sign area, shall be reviewed and approved by the Planning Commission when it is determined that the waivers will accomplish the objectives identified in this section and be consistent with the intent and purpose of the underlying zoning district. 

 Staff response: In any motions made, the Planning Commission and City Commission should specifically address whether or not the requested waivers will accomplish the identified objectives and be consistent with the intent and purpose of the underlying zoning district. 

 The number and dimensions of off-street parking shall be sufficient to meet the minimum required by Section 1704, Parking Requirements. However, where warranted by overlapping or shared parking arrangements, the Planning Commission may grant a waiver reducing the required number of parking spaces. 

 Staff response: The proposed plan provides more than adequate parking for each of the units. The one-family dwellings are provided with a two-car attached garage with each of the multiple-family units having a one-car attached garage. All unit types will have additional dedicated outdoor parking in driveways. 

 All streets and parking areas within the PUD shall meet the minimum construction and other requirements of city ordinances, unless modified by City Commission or Planning Commission, depending upon which body possesses jurisdiction under the City Code. 

 Staff response: No requests to deviate from the minimum construction standards or other requirements have been made by the applicant. All proposed parking and circulation areas within the development are to be privately owned and maintained. 

 Safe, convenient, uncongested, and well-defined vehicular and pedestrian circulation within and to the site shall be provided. Drives, streets, and other elements shall be designed to discourage through traffic, while promoting safe and efficient traffic operations within the site and at its access points. 

 Staff response: The one-family dwellings will be accessed via the surrounding streets in a manner consistent with nearby dwellings while the multiple-family dwellings will be accessed via a 20-foot wide private, internal roadway which will have access points on East 5 th Avenue and Swinton Street. The proposed senior center would share access and access points with the multiple-family dwellings. 

 Sidewalks shall be provided in accordance with the City Complete Streets Resolution dated August 2, 2010. 

 Staff response: The block the school occupies only has a full-length sidewalk along its north side along E 5 th Ave. A partial sidewalk is present on the Swinton side, but only north of its intersection with E 6 th Ave. No sidewalks are present along E 7 th Ave or Superior St. There is a pair of connected approaches at the corner of E 7 th and Swinton, but they don’t connect to any sidewalk segments. As part of the project, the applicant is intending to complete the sidewalk along Swinton and add a full-length sidewalk along the north side of E 7 th Ave. No new sidewalk is planned to serve the four houses on Superior St, however, that should be added to fully comply with the adopted Complete Streets resolution. 

 Landscaping shall be preserved and/or provided to ensure that proposed uses will be adequately buffered from one another and from surrounding public and private property. Plantings and other landscape features shall exceed the standards of Section 1709, Screening, Buffering and Landscaping. 

 Staff response: Detailed landscape plans have not been submitted as part of this application, however, the site is minimally landscaped (aside from grass) with most of the current landscaping consisting of ornamental trees and shrubs near the building. The location of most of those plantings conflicts with the proposed plan, so it seems likely that those would be removed as part of the project. The landscaping shown in the preliminary PUD plan is conceptual in nature and not necessarily an indication of the final layout. The applicant is aware that additional detail will be required. 

 Judicious effort shall be used to preserve significant natural, historical, and architectural features and the integrity of the land, including regulated and nonregulated wetlands. 

 Staff response: The applicant exercised proper due diligence in attempting to adaptively reuse the existing school building, however, it isn’t feasible given its size and configuration. There are no wetlands present on the property. 

 Surface water shall be retained on the site wherever possible. 

 Staff response: The site engineering will move ahead if the preliminary PUD plan is approved, however, the applicant is aware of the requirements. 

 The site shall have adequate lateral support so as to ensure that there will be no erosion of soil or other material. The final determination as to adequacy of, or need for, lateral support shall be made by the City Engineer. 

 Staff response: Staff is confident that no issues will arise in this regard. During the site plan review process, the City’s Engineering Department is part of the review team and will become more involved at that time. 

 Public water and sewer facilities shall be available or shall be provided by the developer as part of the site development. 

 Staff response: Public water and sewer facilities are available and with sufficient capacity to serve the proposed development. 

 Building design shall be of a high quality and exceed the design requirements of the zoning ordinance. 

 Staff response: There are no applicable design requirements; however, the building designs appear to be of high quality and are in keeping with the established characteristics of homes in the surrounding area. 

 Required Notices and Comments Received to Date 

 All required notices have been mailed and published as required by State Statute. As of 9/14/26, numerous comments have been received in opposition to the request and one comment received in favor. 

 BOARDS AND COMMISSION ACTION: 

 The Planning Commission considered this request at their August 27, 2026, regular meeting and, following a Public Hearing, recommended on a 4-1 vote to deny the request. The Planning Commission determined that the application did not satisfy the requirements to change the zoning. The motion recommending denial did not identify specific standards within Section 15C05 of the Zoning Ordinance that were found not to be satisfied. As a result, the Planning Commission's recommendation does not include findings addressing the individual PUD approval criteria contained in the ordinance. 

 Under Section 15C05, the City Commission is authorized to approve, approve with conditions, or deny a proposed Planned Unit Development based upon the standards contained therein. The City Commission's review is therefore conducted independently and should be based upon the record established during the Planning Commission and City Commission Public Hearings, the application materials, public comments, and the applicable approval standards contained in the Zoning Ordinance. 

 From the point of view of staff, the primary issue seemed to be with the multi-family component of the project, however, that component is a use permitted by right in PUDs where the base zoning is R-1. 

 As noted in the staff report above, it is the professional opinion of staff that the application meets all standards and requirements as set forth in the Zoning Ordinance. The staff report as provided to the Planning Commission is included as ATTACHMENT VI . 

 FISCAL IMPACT: 

 No direct fiscal impact accompanies this request, however, the development derived from a potential approval of this request will be subject to property taxes. 

 ALTERNATIVES: 

 The City Commission has the following options to consider on this matter: 
 Schedule the Second Reading for a different date. 
 Direct staff to return with more information. 
 Other Alternative 
 Take no action. 

 Motion & Voting 

 Motion that the City Commission approve a First Reading of the included Ordinance establishing a Planned Unit Development Overlay for the property located at 810 East 5th Avenue, commonly know as the former Lincoln School property and schedule a Second Reading for the October 5, 2026, regular City Commission meeting. This motion is based upon the following findings: 

1. The application satisfies the qualifying the condition of Section 15C02 of the Zoning Ordinance.
2. The application provides multiple demonstrated benefits including a variety of housing types, common open space, and redevelopment if a site exhibiting unique redevelopment constraints. 
3. The proposed development is compatible with the purposes of the Planned Unit Development Overlay as stated in Section 15C and is consistent with the goals and recommendations of the City's Master Plan. 

NO SUPPORT THE MOTION. 

Motion by Andrew Rubinstein, second NONE.

 9. Consideration of a 2% Funding Request to the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians for Community Health Access Coalition (CHAC) for Transition Funding 
 Type 
 Action (Consent) 
 Recommended Action 
 Consideration of a 2% Funding Request to the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians for Community Health Access Coalition (CHAC) for transition funding. 

 BACKGROUND: 
 The City has been approached by Community Health Access Coalition (CHAC) to assist them in securing funding from the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians in the form of a 2% funding request. Community Health Access Coalition is a registered 501c3 non-profit organization coordinating access to healthcare for uninsured residents of Chippewa, Luce, and Mackinac Counties in the Eastern Upper Peninsula of Michigan (EUP). 
 According to the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians website, under the current agreement with the State of Michigan for gaming revenue sharing, 2% of the Tribe's gaming revenue is set aside and made available to local units of government as determined by the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians. The 2% funding program includes an application process for non-government entities to seek funding through the sponsorship of a local unit of government. In this process, the City of Sault Ste. Marie would act as a sponsor for the project, request the funding, then disperse it to the CHAC. 
 ANALYSIS: 
 Included with this item is the application for 2% funding. 
 Community Health Access Coalition is seeking $40,000 from the Sault Tribe’s 2% funding program in order to obtain transition funding. CHAC’s funding through with the Federal Navigator grant was fully discontinued in September 2025. CHAC has been dependent upon grant funds to cover salaries and operating expenses of the agency. CHAC was able to successfully secure a millage for Chippewa County from 2026-2029, however funds will not be available until April 2027. CHAC will exhaust their fund balances before millage funding is available. To ensure CHAC is able to continue operations from December 2026 through April 2027, CHAC needs to secure $50,000. CHAC is requesting 2% funding from Units I, II, and III to meet the operational deficit at 80%, 10%, and 10% respectively based on the client service area and Unit coverage areas. 
 FISCAL IMPACT: 
 There is no direct fiscal impact from this request. If awarded, the City would act as a passthrough agent for the funds to be utilized by CHAC. If Tribal funds are awarded, the Commission will be asked to accept the award and approve a budget amendment in the amount of $40,000 to provide for the payment to CHAC. 
 ALTERNATIVES: 
 List alternatives to the recommended action. 
 The City Commission has the following options to consider on this matter: 
 Adopt resolution with modifications. 
 Direct staff to return with more information. 
 Other Alternative 
 Take no action.

Motion by Ray Bauer, second by Scott Marble.

 Final Resolution: Motion Carried

 Yea: Don Gerrie, Ray Bauer, Jodi Bosbous-Rath, Steve Habusta, Scott Marble, Andrew Rubinstein, Tim Talentino

 Recommended Action

 BACKGROUND AND ANALYSIS: 

 The Police Department is undertaking a project to replace its in-car, body-worn, and interview room camera systems. The existing equipment, purchased in 2016, has exceeded its expected life cycle, resulting in recurring malfunctions and discontinued manufacturer support. Both the in-car and body-worn cameras are experiencing failures, making it increasingly difficult to maintain reliable operation and secure evidence management. 

 To address these issues, the City released a Request for Proposals on September 18, 2025, with proposals due December 5, 2025. The City received vendor proposals and has advanced to field testing of a proposed body-worn camera system. Officers and administrators are evaluating reliability, ease of use, evidence management, redaction, sharing, and compatibility with Department operations. Final vendor selection will follow completion of the evaluation and all applicable City procurement requirements. 

 The body-worn camera portion of the project will initially equip the Department’s 18 current sworn officers and allow the program to expand as vacant positions are filled during the grant period, up to the Department’s authorized staffing level of 24 sworn officers. Each officer will be assigned an individual camera. The project will replace aging equipment, extend reliable camera coverage to detective personnel, and provide secure video capture, storage, redaction, and electronic evidence sharing with the Chippewa County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office and other authorized partners. 

 The Department requests authorization to apply for federal funding through the BJA FY 2026 Body-Worn Camera Policy and Implementation Program for the body-worn camera portion of the larger replacement project. The program supports publicly funded law enforcement agencies seeking to establish, expand, or replace BWC programs. These systems can improve officer safety, strengthen criminal investigations and prosecutions, document officer-citizen encounters, assist with complaint resolution, and improve transparency and accountability. 

 The Department will apply under Category 1: Site-Based Awards to Publicly Funded Law Enforcement Agencies. The expected period of performance is 36 months beginning October 1, 2026. The grant requires a dollar-for-dollar match from non-federal sources and limits federal funding to $2,000 per body-worn camera. 

 The first step of the application process, submission of the SF-424 through Grants.gov, has been completed. The full application must be submitted through JustGrants by October 2, 2026, at 8:59 p.m. Eastern Time. 

 Authorization to apply does not constitute acceptance of a grant award, approval of the required City match, selection of a vendor, authorization to execute a contract, or final approval of the overall camera replacement project. If an award is offered, staff will return to the City Commission for authorization to accept the award, approve the required funding, and take any additional action necessary to proceed. 

 FISCAL IMPACT: 

 The grant application requests $26,438 in federal funding and identifies a potential required City match of $26,438, for a total three-year grant project budget of $52,876. 

 The City’s Capital Improvement Plan budgeted $40,000 in each of FY 2024–2025, FY 2025–2026, and FY 2026–2027 for the overall in-car, body-worn, and interview room camera replacement project. The overall project is planned over five years, with annual funding of $40,000 included or requested through the CIP process to support implementation and ongoing project costs. The proposed grant budget includes only the body-worn camera costs attributable to the grant’s three-year period of performance. 

 No expenditure, budget amendment, or binding commitment of City funds is requested at this time. If the City receives an award, the award and required City match will be presented to the City Commission for acceptance and approval. Final costs will remain subject to vendor selection, contract negotiations, City approval, grant conditions, and applicable federal and local procurement requirements.

 The City Commission has the following options to consider on this matter: 
 Adopt resolution with modifications. 
 Direct staff to return with more information. 
 Other Alternative 
 Take no action.
